core_obligations: Forward implication (proof lines 3372-3373): if F is flat then F tensor_O - is exact, so its satellites vanish and in particular Tor_1^O(F, G) = 0 for every G.
Converse, set up the exact sequence (proof lines 3373-3375): assume Tor_1^O(F, G) = 0 for every G and let G -> H be injective with cokernel Q.
Converse, identify the kernel (proof lines 3375-3380): the long exact sequence of Tor shows that the kernel of F tensor G -> F tensor H is a quotient of Tor_1^O(F, Q), hence zero by hypothesis.
Conclude flatness (proof lines 3380-3381): tensorisation by F preserves injectivity, so F is flat.
proof_roadmap: If F is flat, tensorisation is exact and its satellites vanish.
Conversely, test injectivity of G -> H with cokernel Q.
The long exact Tor sequence exhibits the possible kernel as a quotient of Tor_1(F, Q).
The hypothesis kills it, so tensorisation is exact and F is flat.
difficulty_reason: The lemma is the standard Tor-criterion for flatness on a ringed site (statement lines 3359-3369). The forward direction is the author's one-line consequence of exactness and the vanishing of satellites (proof lines 3372-3373). The converse is the real content: given an injection G -> H with cokernel Q, one must use the long exact sequence of Tor to identify the kernel of F tensor G -> F tensor H as a quotient of Tor_1^O(F, Q), so the hypothesis kills it and tensorisation by F is seen to be exact (proof lines 3373-3381). The point is the exact-sequence bookkeeping that converts the vanishing for the cokernel into exactness at G, which is what makes the criterion usable. The claim is H2: one standard exact-sequence argument after an immediate first direction.
